module_name: M2 Production-Grade Prompting, Agents & Tool Use

cards.front: A prompt's result comes back in the wrong shape (a sentence where you expected a label, prose where you expected JSON). What's the missing technique, and why does it fix this?
cards.back: An output constraint — it controls the form of the response independent of its content. Without one, Claude returns plausible text that a downstream parser was never built to accept.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: Across a multi-turn conversation, Claude's tone or scope keeps drifting and it starts answering a wider question than asked. What's missing from the prompt, and why?
cards.back: A system prompt, or a more specific one — the system prompt sets the behavioral contract (role, scope, format) that should hold for every response regardless of the user turn; if it's too vague, nothing holds those steady as the conversation runs on.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: Claude understands a task correctly but invents an output structure you never specified. What's missing, and why does it fix this?
cards.back: Few-shot examples — Claude can't infer an exact structure from a description alone; one correct input-output pair shows the exact shape to match instead of describing it.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: A prompt produces clean output on the inputs you tested, then breaks on an edge case you didn't anticipate. What does this indicate is missing from the prompt?
cards.back: A constraint covering that variant — the prompt was validated against a narrow set of inputs, and naming the untested variant (or adding an example covering it) closes the gap your test inputs never exposed.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: Why do XML tags matter in a prompt that asks Claude to debug code using supplied documentation?
cards.back: Without tags, the code and the documentation look the same to Claude — wrapping each in descriptive tags (e.g. <my_code>, <docs>) makes the boundary between instructions and input data unambiguous.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: When building few-shot examples for a prompt, where should you source the example pairs from, and how should you mark their boundaries?
cards.back: Pull examples from your highest-scoring evaluation outputs rather than writing them from scratch, and wrap each pair in consistent XML tags (e.g. <sample_input>/<ideal_output>) so the boundary between example and live prompt is clear.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: What mechanism makes Claude's structured outputs (JSON-schema-constrained generation) reliable, as opposed to a prompt-level instruction to 'return JSON'?
cards.back: Constrained decoding — as Claude generates each token, the API only allows tokens that keep the output valid against your schema, so a response violating the schema can't be produced in the first place (a prompt instruction, by contrast, can still slip on an untested edge case).
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: In the Claude API, what does setting strict: true on a tool definition constrain, and when should you reach for it?
cards.back: It constrains the arguments Claude sends to that tool — they're validated against the input schema before your code runs. Reach for it in agentic loops where a malformed tool argument would crash the function or trigger the wrong action.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: What's the latency cost of turning on structured outputs for the first request against a new schema, and how is that cost avoided on later calls?
cards.back: The API has to compile your schema into a grammar before it can constrain output, adding latency on the first call. Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours from last use, so steady traffic on a stable schema pays the compilation cost only once.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: Why does turning on structured outputs increase your input token count, even though you didn't add anything to your own prompt?
cards.back: The API injects its own system prompt describing the expected format when structured outputs are on, and that injected prompt is billed as input tokens like any other.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: Can you combine JSON-schema structured outputs with prefilling the start of Claude's assistant message in the same request?
cards.back: No — JSON outputs and message prefilling are incompatible on the same request. You have to pick whichever technique fits the task.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · System prompts, XML, few-shot, and output constraints

cards.front: In a prompt-iteration trace, a developer's classification prompt keeps getting longer across revision passes without becoming more correct. Independent of accuracy, what side effect starts appearing once the prompt becomes verbose enough, and why?
cards.back: The output itself becomes verbose and unfocused (over 2,000 characters per call), with latency increasing but no accuracy gain — because Claude calibrates its response length and style to match the input; a long, unfocused prompt tends to produce a long, unfocused output.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · The prompt that grew longer instead of better

cards.front: Across six revision passes on a broken classification prompt, a developer added more descriptive paragraphs about each category on every pass, but the parser kept breaking. What was the actual fix, and why didn't the extra description work?
cards.back: The fix was two lines: an output constraint specifying the exact label format, plus a few-shot example covering the ambiguous case. The extra description never worked because it wasn't the missing piece — Claude didn't need a more detailed description of what a billing ticket looks like, it needed to be told the only acceptable response is one word in capital letters.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · The prompt that grew longer instead of better

cards.front: As a rule of thumb, after how many failed re-prompts in a row should you stop adding text to a prompt and diagnose which technique is actually missing?
cards.back: Three re-prompts in a row with no improvement is the signal to stop adding text and diagnose the failure type instead.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · The prompt that grew longer instead of better

cards.front: A system prompt tells Claude to 'extract the key information' from a support ticket into category, urgency, and summary fields, but downstream JSON parsing keeps breaking on inconsistent output. What's the defect, and what does the corrected system prompt need to pin down to fix it for good?
cards.back: A missing output constraint. The fix must specify: the exact field names (category, urgency, summary), the allowed value set for each enum-like field (e.g. category: billing/technical/escalation; urgency: low/medium/high/critical), and an explicit instruction to return only that JSON object with no other text.
cards.extra: M2 · Prompting Craft · Checkpoint 1 · Fix the broken prompt

cards.front: In a streamed Claude response, what is the API actually sending you — is it a live object staying open?
cards.back: No — the API sends a series of small independent events, each describing one change (a block started, content added to it, a block finished, the message finished). Your handler applies each event to the partial state it's building; there's no live object held open on the model's side.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: What does the content_block_start event tell your handler, and what does your handler do with it?
cards.back: It signals a new content block is opening, with its type (text, tool_use, or thinking) and index. Your handler creates a slot at that index for the named block type; a tool_use block opens with its name and id but no input yet.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: Why can't you parse a streamed tool_use block's accumulated input as it arrives via content_block_delta events?
cards.back: The input arrives as a partial JSON string spread across many delta events, and it isn't valid JSON until the block closes at content_block_stop — parsing or running the tool before that point either chokes on malformed JSON or runs with arguments missing.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: What's the first moment a streamed tool_use block's input is complete enough to parse?
cards.back: content_block_stop for that block — that's when the accumulated JSON input is finalized and complete.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: In a streaming Claude response, which event carries the stop_reason, and what should your handler do with it before continuing an agent loop?
cards.back: message_delta carries the stop_reason and final usage counts. Record it and check it before continuing: a stop_reason of tool_use means your assembled tool calls are ready to run; any other value means you're not on the tool-continuation path.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: When should your code add a streamed assistant turn to conversation history — as soon as the read loop exits, or only after a specific event?
cards.back: Only after message_stop arrives, with every block fully assembled. A turn built from a stream cut off partway is incomplete, and if a half-built tool_use block ends up in history, the tool_use pairing rules will reject your next request.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: If a stream is interrupted partway through (dropped connection, timeout, client disconnect) before message_stop arrives, what should your code do with the partial assistant turn it accumulated?
cards.back: Throw it away rather than saving it to history, then retry the request from the last complete turn — committing a half-built turn is exactly what breaks the following request.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Streaming responses and handling partial output without corrupting state

cards.front: In production, a network blip ends a stream after a tool_use block opened and received partial JSON input, but before content_block_stop. The handler appends the turn anyway because its read loop exited normally. Where does the resulting validation error actually surface, and why does that mislead debugging?
cards.back: It surfaces on the NEXT (retry) request, not the interrupted one — because the corrupted turn just sits in history until it's sent again. Teams spend time inspecting the schema and retry logic because that's where the error appears, when the actual defect is upstream in the stream handler, which wrongly treated 'the read loop ended' as equivalent to 'the message is complete.'
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · The stream that left a half-written tool call in the history

cards.front: If a tool-use validation error appears specifically on a retry request (not the original call), what should you check before touching the tool schema?
cards.back: Check whether the prior turn in history was assembled from a stream that got interrupted before message_stop — a half-built block committed from a dropped stream is a common cause of exactly this symptom.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · The stream that left a half-written tool call in the history

cards.front: In a Python stream handler, messages.append(...) runs unconditionally right after the `with client.messages.stream(...) as stream:` block exits, regardless of whether message_stop was seen. What's the concrete fix, and what should happen on the interrupted-stream path instead of appending?
cards.back: Track whether message_stop was seen (e.g. a stop_seen flag). Only append the assembled turn to messages if stop_seen is true; otherwise raise a StreamInterruptedError so the caller retries from the last complete turn instead of the corrupted one being silently added to history.
cards.extra: M2 · Streaming Responses · Checkpoint 4 · Repair the broken stream handler

cards.front: What's the recommended default starting model tier for most production Claude workloads?
cards.back: Sonnet — the balanced default for most production workloads.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: Once you've started on Sonnet, what should actually justify moving up to Opus or down to Haiku, rather than gut feel or pure cost-cutting?
cards.back: An eval set's result, in both directions: move up to Opus only when an eval set shows Sonnet isn't meeting your quality bar; move down to Haiku only when an eval set shows the resulting quality regression is acceptable for the task — not just to save cost. Model choice should always be a measured decision.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: If the input you send to Claude already exceeds the context window before generation even starts, what happens?
cards.back: The Messages API rejects the request outright with a validation error, before generation begins.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: If a request fits within the context window but generation hits the token ceiling partway through, what happens?
cards.back: Current models return the output generated so far, with a model_context_window_exceeded stop reason — a truncated response, not a silently truncated input or a thrown error.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: Why does a Claude agent that ran cleanly through many turns in development sometimes hit its context ceiling much earlier in production?
cards.back: Production tool outputs are often three to five times longer than the small test fixtures used in development, and sessions run for more turns — so the same window fills far earlier in production than it did against short test inputs.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.cloze_text: The four context-budget strategies are {{c1::pruning}} (rewind to an earlier message and drop everything after it), {{c2::compaction}} (summarize history into a condensed version that preserves key learnings), {{c3::clearing}} (start a new conversation with empty context), and {{c4::subagent handoffs}} (delegate a self-contained subtask to an isolated context window that returns only a summary).
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: When should you reach for pruning (rewinding to an earlier message) rather than compaction, and what do you lose by doing it?
cards.back: Reach for pruning after Claude has gone down an unproductive path or accumulated debugging back-and-forth that won't help the next task. You lose all the work done after the rewind point — if Claude learned something useful in that stretch, it has to relearn it.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: What's the key risk of relying on compaction to stay in budget, and where does that risk actually originate when you're writing your own summarizer prompt?
cards.back: Details not captured in the summary become permanently unavailable to Claude going forward. When you write a manual summarizer prompt yourself, what gets preserved depends entirely on how specific that prompt is — an underspecified prompt like 'summarize the conversation' can silently drop task-critical state like which files were modified or what error was resolved.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: What's the difference between clearing context and compaction, in terms of what survives?
cards.back: Clearing starts a new conversation with empty context — nothing from the previous session carries forward at all, so anything Claude needs to remember across sessions must be stored somewhere persistent (like a CLAUDE.md file). Compaction instead summarizes history into a condensed version that keeps the key information, at the cost of losing whatever detail wasn't captured in the summary.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: What does a subagent handoff give up compared to keeping the work in the main agent's own context?
cards.back: Visibility into how the subagent reached its conclusion — the subagent's intermediate steps are discarded along with its isolated context window once it returns its summary result to the parent.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: How does prompt caching reduce cost across a multi-turn session with a stable system prompt and tool schemas?
cards.back: The first request writes a stable prefix of the request to cache; any later request that sends identical content up to that point pays only a fraction of the original processing cost for that prefix, instead of reprocessing it from scratch.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: How do you mark where a prompt-cache breakpoint should be, and how many breakpoints can you set on one request?
cards.back: Set a cache_control field of type ephemeral on the last content block you want cached. You can place up to four breakpoints in a single request.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: What does the count_tokens endpoint let you do that a regular messages call doesn't, and what request body does it take?
cards.back: It measures context pressure before a request goes out, without running inference — it takes the same request body as a messages call but returns just the token count. Use it in development to verify budget assumptions against real tool outputs, and in production to gate requests that would exceed the window before they error.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: In a RAG pipeline, why might a lexical (keyword) search sometimes be run alongside a semantic embedding search rather than relying on embeddings alone?
cards.back: Embedding match retrieves content that's semantically close, which isn't always what contains the exact term you need — a query for a specific identifier can miss the relevant chunk if a more semantically similar (but wrong) result outranks it.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: In RAG chunking, what goes wrong if chunks are split too small, and what goes wrong if they're split too large?
cards.back: Too small, and a chunk lacks the surrounding context to be useful. Too large, and one chunk dilutes the match with unrelated text — a little overlap between chunks helps because facts that cross a chunk boundary would otherwise be split apart and hard to retrieve.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: Between a fetch-once retrieval index and an iterative agentic search across rounds, which approach usually fits better for a stable reference corpus with simple lookups, and which fits better for a changing corpus or multi-step questions?
cards.back: A fetch-once index is worth owning for a stable corpus with simple lookups — you can inspect and test retrieval directly, at the cost of building/maintaining/securing the index. For a changing corpus or multi-step questions, iterative agentic search is usually the simpler system overall, despite costing more tokens and time per query.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Model selection and keeping multi-turn sessions in budget

cards.front: A receipt-processing agent has a team-imposed 40k-token context budget. In development, 20 receipts averaging 800 tokens each stayed comfortably under budget. In production, why did the agent start hitting the cap at turn 8 instead of finishing all 20?
cards.back: Production receipts included extra supporting documentation (transaction records, correspondence), pushing average tool output to about 3,200 tokens per call — 4x the dev fixture size. Eight turns of that alone added roughly 25,600 tokens, and once the system prompt and messages were added on top, the running total hit the team's 40k budget cap well before the task was done.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · The session that ran fine in development, then hit a ceiling in production

cards.front: In the receipts-agent incident, the symptom looked like a tool-selection failure (wrong tools chosen, incomplete analyses). What was the actual root cause, and why did it look like a routing bug?
cards.back: The actual cause was context crowding: accumulated tool outputs that were never pruned pushed the original system prompt and instructions toward the edge of the window, so the agent was deciding without the guidance it started with. It looked like a tool-selection failure because degraded routing is what that crowding produces — the fix was pruning tool outputs and applying compaction proactively, not touching the schema.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · The session that ran fine in development, then hit a ceiling in production

cards.front: In this postmortem, was the 40k-token cap the model's actual context window limit?
cards.back: No — it was a team-imposed cost-control budget on the agent, not the model's ceiling; current Claude API models carry at least a 200k-token window, and the newest flagship models serve 1M tokens by default.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · The session that ran fine in development, then hit a ceiling in production

cards.front: In an agent trace, tool selection is correct for turns 1-4, then turn 5 picks the wrong tool, and turn 6 repeats that exact same wrong choice. What does the repetition at turn 6 tell you, diagnostically, that turn 5 alone wouldn't?
cards.back: It confirms the failure is systemic drift from crowded context, not a one-off fluke — if turn 5's wrong call were a random miss, turn 6 likely wouldn't repeat the identical wrong tool. A consistent, repeated wrong selection right after correct ones is the signature of the context window filling and crowding out the routing instructions, not a fluke in Claude's sampling.
cards.extra: M2 · Context Engineering · Checkpoint 5 · Diagnose the context failure

cards.front: On current Claude models, how do you control how much reasoning effort extended thinking applies to a given request?
cards.back: Through the effort setting — reasoning is adaptive, so you enable it with the thinking parameter and tune depth via the effort level rather than a fixed token budget.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: What happened to the older budget_tokens control for extended thinking, and what happens if you send it to the newest model generations?
cards.back: It's deprecated; on the newest model generations, sending it returns a 400 error.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: By default, can you see the contents of a thinking block from the newest Claude models?
cards.back: No — on the newest models the thinking block's content is omitted by default; you must request a readable summary through the display setting to see it.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: Why shouldn't you enable extended thinking by default on every request, even though it can improve accuracy?
cards.back: Thinking tokens cost the same as output tokens, so running a simple task at high reasoning effort means paying extra for accuracy you don't need — match the tool to the task instead of applying it everywhere.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: For a mechanical task like classification, format conversion, or short factual extraction, should you enable extended thinking? Why?
cards.back: No, leave it off — extended thinking won't improve the answer on a lookup-style task, so you'd just be paying more tokens for nothing. A bare prompt with an output constraint is the right tool.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: When Claude plans across several tool calls in an agentic loop, why does enabling extended thinking for the planning step reduce errors?
cards.back: The reasoning pass is where the model works through dependencies between steps that it would otherwise skip, which reduces wrong-tool selection later in the loop.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: When extended thinking is on and your conversation involves tool use, what must your code do with each thinking block before the next API turn, and why is this a strict requirement rather than a prompting choice?
cards.back: Return it to the API on the next turn exactly as it arrived, unmodified. Each block carries a signature confirming the reasoning wasn't tampered with — editing, summarizing, or dropping it breaks the signature and the API rejects the request. This is a structural/API requirement, not something a prompt change can work around.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: Redacted thinking blocks are encrypted and not meant to be read by humans — does that mean your code can skip returning them on the next turn?
cards.back: No — redacted thinking blocks follow the same carry-back rule as regular thinking blocks; they still must be returned untouched even though their contents aren't human-readable.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: If accumulated reasoning from thinking blocks is bloating your context window in a tool-use loop, what's the correct fix?
cards.back: Apply context-engineering techniques (like pruning or compaction) to manage the accumulation — not by stripping or editing the thinking blocks themselves, since that breaks their signature and gets the next request rejected.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Extended Thinking: Turning reasoning on, calibrating effort, and reading it back correctly

cards.front: You need to classify 50,000 support tickets into three labels overnight. Should you enable extended thinking for this job, and what's the cost risk if you do?
cards.back: Leave it off — a one-word label needs no reasoning pass, and reasoning tokens applied to every single ticket multiply your output cost across all 50,000 calls with no accuracy gain.
cards.extra: M2 · Extended Thinking · Checkpoint 2 · Decide when extended thinking earns its cost

cards.front: What's the most common misconception about how tool-use works with Claude, and what's actually true?
cards.back: That Claude runs the tools itself. In fact Claude only reads your tool definitions, decides which one fits, and tells your application what to call along with the input arguments — your application has to execute the tool and send the result back.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: After Claude returns a tool_use block, is it holding a connection open waiting for your code to execute the tool?
cards.back: No — the assistant turn has already ended and the model is stateless between calls. Your code executes the tool, then makes a fresh API request containing the prior messages plus the tool result to continue.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: What's the API-enforced pairing rule between a tool_use block and its tool_result, and what happens if it's violated?
cards.back: Every tool_use block in an assistant turn must be answered by a tool_result block with a matching ID in the immediately following user turn. If the IDs don't match, the result is missing, or the turns are out of order, the request fails validation — this is structural, not something a prompt change can fix.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: When Claude returns a text block alongside a tool_use block in the same assistant turn, what must your code do when appending that turn to conversation history, and what breaks if you don't?
cards.back: Preserve the full content array, including the text block. Dropping the text block corrupts the context Claude relies on for follow-up turns.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: Of the three parts of a tool schema (name, description, input_schema), which one determines whether Claude selects the tool correctly, and what's the difference between a weak and a strong version of it?
cards.back: The description. A weak one just says 'use this to find information,' which Claude can't distinguish from any other retrieval tool. A strong one states both when to use it and when not to — e.g. 'use this to retrieve the current balance for a specific account ID, and do not use this for transaction history' — giving Claude an exclusion condition.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: In a tool's input_schema, when should a parameter be marked required versus left optional?
cards.back: Mark it required only when the call doesn't make sense without it — required forces Claude to fabricate a value it has no basis for if the field doesn't actually apply. Leave it optional (with a default in your function signature) when the tool can operate without it, so Claude can omit what it doesn't have instead of guessing.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: When one tool's output feeds directly into the next tool call's input, how should you structure the two calls, and why?
cards.back: As separate sequential turns — the second call's input can't be built until the first call's result comes back, so a real dependency has to run in sequence rather than in parallel.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: By default, how do current Claude models handle multiple independent tool calls, and what setting forces exactly one tool call per turn instead?
cards.back: They default to issuing them as parallel tool_use blocks within a single turn, which your code can execute concurrently. Set disable_parallel_tool_use to force strictly one tool call per turn.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: Roughly how much description should you write per tool, and what happens if you write too little versus too much?
cards.back: Three to four sentences covering what it does, when Claude should reach for it, and what it returns, with examples of valid inputs where format matters. Too short and Claude guesses because there isn't enough signal; too long and the trigger conditions get buried under detail Claude doesn't reference at decision time.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and what problem does it solve compared to writing tool schemas yourself?
cards.back: A standardized communication layer that moves tool definitions and execution out of your application code and into dedicated servers. Instead of writing and maintaining a schema and execution function for every operation yourself, you connect to an existing MCP server and Claude selects among its tools using the same description-based routing.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: What's the practical context-window cost of connecting several MCP servers to a session at once, even if you don't use most of their tools that turn?
cards.back: Every connected server's tool definitions get added to the context window regardless of whether they're used in the current turn — so tool definitions alone can consume budget before the first message even arrives. Register only the servers you're actively using.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: In the API MCP Connector's mcp_toolset configuration, what do the defer_loading and enabled settings each control?
cards.back: defer_loading (in default_config or a per-tool config) delays loading a tool's definition until the model actually needs it, cutting upfront context cost for a server with a large tool list. enabled turns individual tools on or off, so you can register a server but expose only the tools you want the model to see.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: What are the two transports MCP servers can run over, and which one applies to local versus remote servers?
cards.back: Local servers use stdio, where your application spawns the server as a subprocess and talks over standard input/output. Remote servers use Streamable HTTP, with POST for client-to-server messages and an optional GET-based SSE stream for server-initiated messages (an older SSE-only transport is deprecated).
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Tool Schemas Claude Selects Correctly: Definition, Loop, and Calling Patterns

cards.front: An agent keeps calling search_docs when the answer is already in context, even after several retries. Both search_docs and get_context_summary have descriptions that essentially say 'use this to find/retrieve information.' What's actually wrong, and is rewording just one of the two tools' descriptions enough to fix it?
cards.back: The two descriptions look identical to Claude's tool-selection reasoning, so it has no reliable signal to distinguish them. No — both tools need the boundary added: each description needs one sentence naming when it should be used and one naming when it should not be used (e.g. search_docs excludes cases already answered in-session; get_context_summary excludes cases requiring new lookups).
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · The description that sent Claude to the wrong tool

cards.front: If two tools' descriptions still can't be cleanly separated even after adding exclusion conditions to both, what's the recommended fix?
cards.back: Merge them into a single tool with a type parameter instead of trying to keep maintaining two overlapping tools.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · The description that sent Claude to the wrong tool

cards.front: In a tool-use trace, the assistant issues a tool_use block with id='toolu_01', but the following user turn's tool_result block references tool_use_id='toolu_02'. What error does the API return, and how does the API actually match tool_result to tool_use blocks?
cards.back: invalid_request_error: 'tool_result block references unknown tool_use_id.' The API matches tool_use and tool_result blocks by ID, not by position/order — so a mismatched ID is treated as referencing a tool_use block that doesn't exist in the conversation at all. Fix: return the result with the exact same ID the assistant issued.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Checkpoint 3 · Spot and fix the schema bug

cards.front: In the tool_result block convention, why is a tool_result always sent with role='user' even though your application code (not a person) generated its content?
cards.back: The role field marks who is sending the message to Claude, not who authored the content — tool_result content is generated by your application but is still sent in the user role by convention.
cards.extra: M2 · Tool-use and Schema Design · Checkpoint 3 · Spot and fix the schema bug

cards.front: What's the core question you should answer before deciding to build an agent, rather than a simpler pattern, for a task?
cards.back: Whether you can enumerate the exact steps in code. If you can, a workflow is the right call; an agent is for when you can specify the goal and the tools but not the exact path between them — and agents carry coordination overhead and more failure surface than simpler patterns, so this decision should be made deliberately, not by default.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: What's the difference between the 'agent pattern' itself and the 'wiring path' you choose to implement it, and does the pattern change based on which wiring path you pick?
cards.back: The agent pattern (a loop that calls tools, manages context, and runs until a goal is met) stays constant across all three wiring paths for single-agent systems. What changes between paths is how much of that loop you write yourself versus hand off to a library or hosted service — not the pattern itself.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: In the raw Messages API loop wiring path, what do you own, and what's the tradeoff of choosing it?
cards.back: You own the full loop: tool execution, context management, retries, and exit conditions — nothing is provided for you. Choose it when you need full control or have constraints a library doesn't accommodate, but every behavior an SDK would give for free becomes code you write and test yourself.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: When using the Agent SDK, what configuration must you explicitly set, rather than rely on a default, to control whether filesystem-based settings like CLAUDE.md and Skills load?
cards.back: settingSources — you must set it explicitly to the sources you intend (e.g. ["user", "project", "local"] to match Claude Code CLI behavior, or [] to run fully isolated), and confirm current default behavior against the Agent SDK reference at build time rather than assuming.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: With Claude Managed Agents, who runs the iteration loop and the execution sandbox, and what does your application do instead?
cards.back: Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox server-side. Your application defines the agent once (model, system prompt, tools, MCP servers, skills), references it by ID, sends user events, and streams results back over server-sent events.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: Why are Claude Managed Agent sessions currently ruled out for PHI workloads or Zero Data Retention (ZDR) requirements, regardless of how well the pattern otherwise fits?
cards.back: Managed Agent sessions are stateful and stored server-side, and that storage means they aren't currently eligible for Zero Data Retention or a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement — so PHI/ZDR workloads have to route to the Agent SDK or a raw loop on a covered configuration instead.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.cloze_text: The four steps that hold across every agent wiring path are: {{c1::register tools}} (so Claude knows what's available), {{c2::set the system prompt}} (scoped to the agent's specific task, not broad), {{c3::handle the tool-use loop}} (your code executes every tool call and returns a tool-result), and {{c4::define exit conditions}} (so the loop doesn't run indefinitely waiting for Claude to volunteer to stop).
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: Why does scoping an agent's system prompt narrowly to its specific task, rather than writing a broad one, improve reliability?
cards.back: A broad system prompt produces broader, less reliable tool routing. A system prompt that names the specific task and the tools available for it produces more consistent tool-selection behavior.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.cloze_text: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints have three main insertion points based on risk: {{c1::before a destructive tool call}} (high risk — irreversible actions that can't be undone), {{c2::after a planning step}} (medium risk — an incorrect plan would produce the wrong outcome even if every step executes correctly), and {{c3::on unexpected output}} (variable risk — catches failure modes retry logic alone won't resolve).
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: What question should you ask to decide whether a given step in an agent loop needs a human-in-the-loop checkpoint?
cards.back: What is the worst possible outcome if this step runs without a human check? The answer to that question determines whether — and where — a HITL checkpoint is required.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: What's the more common tooling mistake in production agents: registering too many tools 'just in case,' or too few tools?
cards.back: Over-tooling is more common. Teams register every tool they might conceivably need, and Claude's tool-selection quality degrades as the tool surface grows. Start with the minimum tools required for the task and add more only when a specific capability gap is confirmed.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: For attorney-client-privileged work, what kind of Claude API access setup typically survives a code review?
cards.back: Direct API/SDK calls from inside the firm's own application, authenticated via SSO and routed through a firm-approved LLM gateway with full request/response logging.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: For attorney-client-privileged work routed through direct API access, what must the firm itself still build, since Anthropic doesn't provide it by default?
cards.back: Its own conversation logging in the application layer — Anthropic's Compliance Conversation content (prompts, responses, tool call payloads) is not captured by Anthropic by default on direct API traffic, so the firm must implement and route that logging to an approved destination itself.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: For GDPR/data-residency requirements, why does defaulting to Anthropic's direct API, rather than a cloud-mediated route, typically break the requirement?
cards.back: The direct Anthropic API does not currently provide EU data residency and doesn't let you pin the region of model execution — partners with EU data-residency requirements need to route through a cloud-mediated path like Bedrock or Vertex instead, pinning the region in the client configuration to a covered jurisdiction.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Building a production agent: the loop, wiring paths, orchestration, and human-in-the-loop

cards.front: A config-editing agent (read_file/write_file/validate_config, up to 10 retry iterations) worked flawlessly in every test case. In production, it correctly fixed an out-of-range rate-limit parameter, validate_config passed, and the loop exited cleanly after one iteration exactly as designed — yet it caused an outage. What was actually wrong, given the loop worked exactly as designed?
cards.back: The exit condition itself was the problem, not the loop. validate_config only checked that the new value was within the schema's allowed range — it was never designed to check whether downstream systems depended on the old value. There was no checkpoint between 'validation passed on this file' and 'write committed to the customer environment,' so a schema-valid write still broke a production dependency validate_config could never see.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · The agent that edited a production file

cards.front: Why did testing never surface the need for a human-in-the-loop checkpoint before this agent's write_file call reached a customer environment?
cards.back: Testing ran against a disposable scratch directory where nothing a 'wrong write' touched actually mattered — so the gap between 'proposing a change' and 'committing a change' never produced a consequence in testing, only in production where the write hit a real, load-bearing configuration.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · The agent that edited a production file

cards.front: What design-time question would have caught the missing HITL checkpoint in the config-editing agent before the incident happened?
cards.back: 'What is the worst possible outcome if write_file runs without a human check?' — that question, asked while scoping the tool surface at design time (not after the first incident), determines whether a checkpoint is required before an irreversible action executes.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · The agent that edited a production file

cards.front: For an update_record tool that modifies a customer record's field, what should its description say beyond just what it does, to keep Claude from calling it too eagerly?
cards.back: It should state the precondition and the exclusion, in the model's own routing language — e.g. 'Only call this after a read_record call has confirmed the current value and the proposed change has been reviewed. Do not use this for bulk updates or schema changes.' A bare 'updates a field' description would let the agent call it whenever it merely inferred an update was needed, without confirming the current value first.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Checkpoint 6 · Complete the agent wiring

cards.front: In an agent loop that gates a specific tool (e.g. update_record) behind human approval, where exactly must the approval check sit relative to execute_tool, and why is approving after execution too late?
cards.back: The check must sit inside the per-block loop, gating on the tool name, before execute_tool runs for that block — so read_record calls pass through unchanged while update_record calls pause for approval first. Approving after execute_tool has already run is too late because the irreversible write has already happened by the time the human sees the approval prompt.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Construction · Checkpoint 6 · Complete the agent wiring

cards.front: What are the two opposite-direction failure modes of choosing the wrong memory scope for an agent?
cards.back: Too much state kept in-context inflates every API call, since the model re-reads the full conversation every turn and cost scales with session length. Too little state kept in persistent storage strips the agent of memory across sessions, since anything not written down disappears the moment the conversation ends.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: For a task-execution agent that receives one job, finishes it, and closes out — with no follow-up expected — which memory scope fits, and what's the overhead?
cards.back: No persistent memory (stateless) — each session is fully independent, so there's no retrieval or storage overhead at all, since there's nothing to save.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: For an agent that has to continue the same thread across multiple days for the same user, which memory scope is required, and what does that scope cost you?
cards.back: External storage — state is written to a database and read back at session start. It costs retrieval latency on each call and the engineering work of building read/write logic, but it's the only scope where state actually survives a session ending.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: What's the tradeoff of summarized memory (a condensed version of prior conversation injected at the next session's start) versus replaying full history?
cards.back: It costs fewer tokens per session than replaying full history, but the summarization step drops whatever detail wasn't preserved — the agent only ever sees what the summarization prompt chose to keep.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: Why does the default path of 'just store the full conversation history and send it on every call' tend to work at first and then fail later, rather than failing immediately?
cards.back: It works while sessions are short, but token cost scales with every additional turn and latency climbs as the window fills — eventually a long session hits the hard context limit and the agent stops responding, forcing an under-pressure refactor to external storage instead of having chosen the right scope up front.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: What is a Skill (SKILL.md), and how is its context cost fundamentally different from CLAUDE.md's?
cards.back: A Skill is a reusable markdown file that teaches Claude how to handle a specific kind of task once; it loads automatically only when a request matches its description, so its instructions never enter context unless relevant. CLAUDE.md, by contrast, loads into every session unconditionally in the Claude Code CLI, at a fixed cost regardless of whether that turn's task needs it.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: A SKILL.md file has two parts. What are they, and which one is the actual matching criterion Claude uses to decide whether to load the full instructions?
cards.back: A frontmatter block (name + description) and the instructions below it. The description is the matching criterion — Claude compares every available Skill's name and description against your request, and only loads the full instructions when there's a match.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: In the Agent SDK specifically, what controls whether CLAUDE.md and other filesystem settings load into a session, and what should you do rather than assume a default?
cards.back: The settingSources configuration controls it. Don't rely on a default — set it explicitly to the sources you intend, and confirm current default behavior against the Agent SDK reference at build time.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: When you delegate work to a subagent, do Skills and permission context both carry over automatically from the parent session, or does the behavior differ between the two?
cards.back: It differs: subagents do NOT automatically inherit Skills or conversation history from the parent — they start with a clean context, and any Skill the subagent needs must be explicitly listed in its own configuration. But subagents DO inherit the parent session's permission context; permission scope is not reset at delegation.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Choosing the right scope for state that survives sessions

cards.front: An escalation-support agent used in-context memory and worked fine in development (single continuous 10-15 turn sessions). In production it used many shorter sessions across more days instead. Why did in-context memory fail here even though each individual session was short?
cards.back: Because state accumulated ACROSS sessions, not within one — by session four, the injected in-context history from prior sessions exceeded 40,000 tokens before the agent even processed its first tool call. In-context memory is scoped to handle one long session growing, not many short sessions whose histories keep getting re-injected and stacking on top of each other.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · The agent that filled the window on session four

cards.front: In the session-four incident, once injected history plus system prompt plus tool schemas passed 45,000 tokens before the first productive turn, what symptom did the team see, and what did they initially misattribute it to?
cards.back: The agent began returning incomplete results as its remaining budget was exhausted mid-analysis — a symptom that initially looked like a tool-selection failure, when the actual cause was the memory architecture (accumulated in-context history), not the tool schemas.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · The agent that filled the window on session four

cards.front: A coding assistant works with a developer across a single multi-hour session that won't continue afterward. Why is in-context memory the right scope here, rather than either external storage or summarized memory?
cards.back: The session already fits inside one context window and won't outlive itself, so external storage would be unneeded read/write overhead for state that's never reused. Summarized memory would actively hurt here — compressing the session would discard exact code-level detail the developer still needs to reference later in that same session.
cards.extra: M2 · Agent Memory · Checkpoint 7 · Choose the right memory pattern

cards.front: In a buggy agent-loop implementation, the assistant's turn is committed to history via a filtered assemble(blocks) call that drops any 'thinking' block, and the commit happens unconditionally rather than being gated on message_stop. What two separate defects does this single line of code cause, and how do they interact?
cards.back: Two independent defects layered together: (1) committing before message_stop can write a half-built tool_use block into history if the stream was interrupted, and (2) stripping the thinking block breaks the extended-thinking carry-back rule even on a complete stream, since the signature the API expects to see again is now missing. Either defect alone breaks the next request; together, an API rejection could stem from either cause, so both must be fixed, not just one.
cards.extra: M2 · Cumulative Debug Task · Cumulative debug task · Identify each bug

cards.front: In the cumulative debug exercise, what four distinct layers can a single planted bug belong to in a production Claude agent implementation, and what's the diagnostic value of checking all four rather than assuming the layer where the error message appears?
cards.back: The schema layer (tool descriptions/definitions), the streaming layer (response assembly and history commits), the context layer (message structure/block pairing), and the memory layer (what state persists across sessions). The diagnostic value is that an API error surfacing at one layer (e.g. a context-layer validation error) often traces back to a defect actually introduced in a different layer (e.g. the streaming layer failing to gate a commit on message_stop) — so a systematic layer-by-layer check catches root causes a symptom-first search would miss.
cards.extra: M2 · Cumulative Debug Task · Cumulative debug task · Identify each bug

cards.front: What's the formula for how many visual tokens an image costs Claude, based on its pixel dimensions?
cards.back: ceil(width / 28) × ceil(height / 28) visual tokens — Claude views images in patches, where each 28×28-pixel block is one visual token.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: Roughly how many visual tokens does a 1,000 × 1,000 pixel image cost, and what does that mean in practical terms for a pipeline sending several such images per request?
cards.back: About 1,296 visual tokens (ceil(1000/28) × ceil(1000/28) = 36 × 36 patches). At that rate, ten high-resolution screenshots in one request can consume as much context as a detailed system prompt — so image token cost has to be calculated at design time, not discovered after deployment.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: If an image you send exceeds a model's maximum native resolution (long-edge limit or visual-token limit), what happens to it before processing, and what does that mean for calculating its token cost?
cards.back: It gets downscaled before processing — so the visual-token formula (ceil(width/28) × ceil(height/28)) has to be run on the scaled dimensions, not the original ones, to get an accurate cost estimate.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: Comparing inline base64 image encoding to the Files API: when is inline base64 the right choice, and when does it become the wrong one?
cards.back: Inline base64 is right for one-off images where adding an upload step would add complexity without payoff. It becomes the wrong choice once the same image gets sent repeatedly, since the full encoded payload travels with the request every single time, multiplying transfer cost.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: What's the main dependency risk of referencing an image by a public URL rather than uploading it, and when should you avoid URL references?
cards.back: Claude fetches the URL at request time, so the URL has to be stable, public, and reachable at that exact moment. Avoid URL references for anything behind auth, anything with a short-lived signed expiry, or anything you can't guarantee will be reachable when the request runs.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: With the Files API, what's the one-time cost versus the ongoing cost of sending the same image across many requests?
cards.back: You pay the upload cost once to get a file_id back. Every later request then carries just that ID instead of the image bytes, so payload overhead drops to near-zero on every request after the first.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: For sending a PDF to Claude, what content block type is used, and does its source structure differ from an image block's?
cards.back: The block type is `document` (not `image`), but the source structure follows the same pattern as images — base64, a URL, or a Files API file_id all work the same way.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: Is a name field required on a PDF document block, and what optional fields does it support instead?
cards.back: No, there's no required name field. It accepts an optional title field for a readable document name and an optional context field for additional metadata — neither is required to send a PDF.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: Why does a bare 'describe this image' prompt tend to produce shallow output, and what kind of ambiguity does a good visual-analysis prompt need to name explicitly that a text-only prompt never has to?
cards.back: It produces shallow output for the same reason a bare text prompt does — Claude has no target structure to aim for. A visual prompt additionally needs to name how to handle ambiguity unique to images: overlapping objects, depth/spatial relationships, and partial occlusion (e.g. 'if objects overlap, describe each separately and note the overlap').
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: What's the maximum size of a single Message Batches API call, in terms of request count and total size?
cards.back: Up to 100,000 requests or 256 MB, whichever limit is hit first.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: How does per-token pricing compare between the Message Batches API and the synchronous API, and what's the tradeoff you accept for that lower cost?
cards.back: Batch per-token cost is lower than synchronous. The tradeoff is latency: batch processing is non-deterministic and can take up to 24 hours (often much faster), so it suits offline pipelines and evaluation runs, not real-time user interactions.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Images, PDFs, and high-volume processing

cards.front: A developer splits a large nightly classification job into smaller chunks and loops over the synchronous API calling each item individually, but still hits rate limits. Why doesn't chunking the input list fix this?
cards.back: Chunking a list and looping over the synchronous API is not batching — it's serialization with extra steps. The API still sees one request per item, back to back, producing the exact same number of calls (and the same rate-limit exposure) as the un-chunked version. The Message Batches API is a genuinely different submission model, not just a smaller batch size.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · The batch job that was not actually a batch

cards.front: When you submit work through the Message Batches API, do results come back in the same order the requests were submitted, and how do you correctly match each result back to its input?
cards.back: No — results return in arbitrary order, not submission order. Use the custom_id field you set on each request to match results back to their corresponding inputs.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · The batch job that was not actually a batch

cards.front: When choosing how to send an image/document asset to Claude — inline base64, the Files API, or (for volume) the Message Batches API — what's the single deciding factor that determines which one fits?
cards.back: The asset's reuse pattern and request volume: a one-off asset used in a single request goes inline; an asset reused across multiple requests goes to the Files API once and is referenced by file_id thereafter; and bulk, non-interactive volume (thousands of inputs, no one waiting) goes through the Batches API regardless of whether the individual assets are reused.
cards.extra: M2 · Multimodal and Batch Ingestion · Checkpoint 8 · Select the right input encoding for each scenario

cards.front: How does the Claude Agent SDK differ from the plain Anthropic SDK?
cards.back: The Claude Agent SDK (distributed as @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk for TypeScript, claude-agent-sdk for Python) gives programmatic access to the same agent loop that powers Claude Code — iteration, tool execution, observation, termination — so you can embed an agent in your own product. The Anthropic SDK, by contrast, is just a thin convenience wrapper over the API and does not run an agent loop at all.
cards.extra: M2 · Module Wrap-up · Key terms from this module

cards.front: What is SOC 2, and who typically cites it?
cards.back: Service Organization Control 2 — an audit framework developed by the AICPA for evaluating how a service organization handles customer data. It's the standard most commonly cited when a SaaS vendor or cloud service provider is asked to demonstrate their security practices meet a recognized bar.
cards.extra: M2 · Module Wrap-up · Key terms from this module

cards.cloze_text: An agent's **state** — the information it carries between turns — consists of {{c1::the conversation so far}}, {{c2::what the user asked for}}, and {{c3::results from earlier tool calls}}.
cards.extra: M2 · Module Wrap-up · Key terms from this module

cards.front: In the Messages API, what do the two stop_reason values most relevant to agentic loops, end_turn and tool_use, each signal?
cards.back: end_turn means Claude has finished and isn't requesting any further action. tool_use means Claude has issued one or more tool_use blocks and is waiting for your code to return results before it continues.
cards.extra: M2 · Module Wrap-up · Key terms from this module

cards.front: Why should you avoid relying on a fixed 'characters per token' rule of thumb when estimating Claude's token usage?
cards.back: The characters-per-token average depends on the specific model's tokenizer, and tokenizers differ between model generations — so treat any chars-per-token estimate as model-dependent and confirm current tokenizer behavior at build time rather than treating it as a constant.
cards.extra: M2 · Module Wrap-up · Key terms from this module
